source.title: One system for learning and remembering episodes and rules
source.citation: Joshua T. S. Hewson et al., 2024
source.authors: Joshua T. S. Hewson; Sabina J. Sloman; Marina Dubova

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model capacity and reports accuracy differences across capacity regimes, bearing conceptually on whether performance improves beyond sufficient capacity. It does not measure a full double-descent curve.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent work as background, but does not test error across epochs or sample sizes, nor test noise- or regularization-dependent peaks. Its own capacity comparisons are reported; the additional forgetting result is recorded as a finding that fits none of the listed double-descent versions.
record.test_reason: Weak, coarse test in a new setting, an associative-learning MLP task. Capacity is swept at 0.5, 1, 10 and 100 times the memorization threshold. Generalization (Atest–C) is measured, and excess-capacity models beat sufficient (interpolation-threshold) and constrained models. This bears on the second descent past interpolation in V1. The four-point sweep and the lack of reported numbers cannot show a peak at the threshold. The authors frame the result as 'consistent with' Belkin and Nakkiran rather than as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that one system with excess representational capacity can both learn and remember episodes and rules. This challenges the view that these are inherently competing processes requiring complementary learning systems.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a two-hidden-layer MLP in an associative-learning and forgetting task, comparing discrete capacity regimes rather than measuring the original double-descent risk curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The experiments vary noise level and capacity regime; the text reports that excess capacity performs better across the tested cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Excess-capacity MLPs retained previously learned episodes and rules better after training on interfering associations (p<.001).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Excess capacity beyond the memorization threshold reduces catastrophic forgetting in sequential associative learning.

record.problems: The text provides no numerical accuracy values for the capacity comparisons, and the reported capacity regimes do not establish a complete double-descent curve.

untested.parts: Whether test error peaks near the sufficient-capacity (1x) model; no fine-grained size sweep is run.
Epoch-wise test-error shape is not analysed; Fig. 1 shows learning and forgetting curves only.
Sample size is fixed at 10 and not varied.
Only one model class (MLP) is tested; there is no cross-class comparison.
Noise is varied, but its effect on a peak is not reported; regularization is not tested.
No re-counting of parameters is tested.

missing.what: Per-capacity (0.5x, 1x, 10x, 100x) and per-noise-level test (Atest–C) accuracy values. These would be needed to see whether 1x is worse than 0.5x, i.e. a peak at the interpolation threshold.
A separate row for Block 1 generalization to Atest–C (test), distinct from Atrain–B memorization (train).

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a short (roughly 2-page) conference abstract. Its results are stated only qualitatively, with p-values and no numbers. Double descent is invoked as background, and the capacity result is described as 'consistent with prior literature'. The verdict therefore rests on a thin, qualitative statement.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep measuring a fall-rise-fall test-error curve or a peak near the training-set interpolation threshold.
Training-time results concern learning and forgetting, not fall-rise-fall test error over epochs.
Training sample count is not varied.
The study compares capacity regimes in one MLP setting; it does not establish a full U-shaped curve or test the claim across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs, and sample count.
Noise levels are varied, but the study does not test whether label noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether tuned regularization removes them.
No alternative effective-parameter count or re-expression of a second descent as a U-shaped curve is tested.

rows.subject: simple multi-layer perceptron architecture with two hidden layers of equal width
rows.size_stated: capacities of .5, 1, 10 and 100 times the capacity needed to fully memorize the datasets
rows.operation_detail: Compared constrained, sufficient, and excess capacity regimes.

conditions.value: learning episodes and rules; results at the end of training

rows.measure: Mean classification accuracy for learning episodes and rules
rows.value: Models with excess capacity were better able than models with constrained and sufficient capacity to learn both episodes and rules; pairwise mean comparisons were significant at p < 0.001.
rows.uncertainty: p < 0.001 for pairwise comparisons; error bars show standard errors
rows.note: The text reports the comparison across capacity regimes and varying noise, but supplies no numerical accuracy values. This supports improved performance in the tested excess-capacity regime, not a complete double-descent curve.
rows.check: Relinked from V4 to V1, since the subject is a single neural-network class (two-hidden-layer MLP), not a cross-model-class test. The measure mixes training-set memorization (Atrain–B episodes) with test generalization (Atest–C rules); only the latter is test error and should be its own row. The text gives no accuracy values. It reports only that excess beats constrained and sufficient. Whether 1x is worse than 0.5x (the peak) cannot be read. The state is partial because the improvement beyond the threshold appears but the fall-rise shape is not shown.
